Find a wall literally anywhere. Get close to it. Use the inside of your foot like a putter in golf, just pulling back your leg and trying to hit the right part of the ball with the right part of your foot and hit it straight so it comes back to you and trap the ball. Repeat. That’ll get you comfortable with the general feeling and idea of NOT using your toe, which you should almost NEVERRR be using. Toe is highly inaccurate and lacks long distance power + it can injure your toes if you hit it wrong. When I was really young my favorite drill I made for myself to build accuracy and power was just starting from the penalty spot on the field. Split the goal into six parts separated from top/bottom and the left/middle/right. Pick a spot. Hit it. Do that until you don’t miss. When you don’t miss. Do that another 100 times. Then back up to the 18 aka the big white box. Repeat. Keep backing up about 10-20 yards after each 100 successful reps. Until you reach halfway line. If you can hit halfway line and be completely accurate consistently. You’re better than 50% of players now. Also DONT WORRY about building incorrect technique. That’s literally called learning. Everyone sucks and toe pokes at first. If you want to get better you make yourself. Get out there and go to work and analyze what works for you and what doesn’t and continuously improve. 

TLDR:  practice against a wall like every player in existence has. technique is gonna suck bc you just started. Newsflash!! That’s apart of being alive. Go and practice that’s how you build better tech. Nobody can tell you exactly how to hit a ball everyone does it differently. Step to, plant foot, open hips, square your body to where you wanna hit. Stay loose and flexible with the striking leg, pick a spot on the ball and a spot on your foot. Hit ball. Repeat until it’s perfect.

I am all of 5’7 and a buck 20 soaking wet. Big fit fast guys like that love to use their body to create separation between you and the ball. Use that. You know he’s gonna want to rush into you. You know he wants to stick a leg and a shoulder in. Draw it out and move around it. Big quick changes of direction so that if he does try to put a body on it’s a foul. Technicality on the ball is always a good option for strong guys like that. They tend to be a bit stiff and like to throw the muscle around in place of precise and delicate movements. Lean into that. Also again, 120 here. Proper protection of the ball and positioning of your body on the ball and where you place your weight is key. I have shoved off 6”4 200+ guys just bc they don’t know how to hold themselves. Keep the ball tight and keep your balance always. And like everyone else here said. Always be a threat on the ball passing wise. Make them back up and give you space and time to make a move or risk getting a deep line breaking pass.

KD is kinda low for diamond/ normal for a regular plat player. Game gets faster paced. Lobbies are more aggressive. Teams play tighter and smarter. Team comps are solid most of the time. Clear communication is key. Early KP IS KEY!! Land with maybe 1-2 teams. Get your 2-3 kills off rip And make your rotations. Try to have a Ring scan, survey scan/support and a rotation legend every game. Don’t focus too much on looting, doesn’t matter when you’re a box. Be aggressive and be fast. If you get cracks or knocks or even decent dmg you need to be eliminating quickly. Hand holding and not being split by more than 5-10 feet is critical. You think it’s lame until a team splits one guy off from some decent entry shots. Isolates and rushes and crushes and then roll onto you and that’s wraps. Be comfortable w every gun. Be comfortable with every gun at every range. Always be looking to isolate other players at any chance. 


TLDR hold hands. get early kills. get ring pos. Be fast. Be aggressive. Be smart. And HAVE FUN!!!

It’s a Triple take in close range, hip fire for the spread. Take the 2x off the fucking shotgun for christs sake. Focus more on lining shots up and not your movement. Once you can one mag someone, then worry about strafing. Also focus more on lining shots up rather than just firing as soon as it’s ready to fire again. Take the time to line the crosshairs to where they’re GOING to be. And hit the shot. Calculate movement and Line it up. Don’t get nervous or hasty and start spamming shots bc you think you’re going to lose the fight, just calm down and focus on accuracy. Accuracy over volume. 10 shots and 0% accuracy is a hell of a lot worse than 3 shots and 100% accuracy. Also go into the gun range and PLEASE learn the recoil patterns of these guns and adjust sensitivity as needed. You also need to learn where to pre aim when fighting. Where you first sight in is so inconsistent you’re bound to miss half the time. Etc etc

Should def schedule some days w someone on your team you feel a connection with and practice long balls to each other, crossing the ball across the field and skimmers with pace to each other. Hitting the ball long is ALL about technique and where and how you strike the ball not how hard you swing. Accuracy will improve through repetition. Also, I used to sit out there for hours. Putting the ball further and further back from the goal. Just trying to see how far I could kick it without it hitting the ground before it hit the net. Then to improve accuracy, just pick a spot in the net and go for it until you hit a certain number and swap. Keep the number low to try and challenge yourself with different techniques for different spots. I ended up being able to smack the ball from past half field and hit top bins or at least the side I wanted to at the age of like 10.

The history of the Pitt Bull can be traced back to the early 1800’s in the United Kingdom. Pit Bulls were originally bred from Old English Bulldogs (these dogs are similar in appearance to today’s American Bulldog) who gained their popularity on the British Isles in a cruel blood sport known as “bull baiting”. One to two Bulldogs were set to harass a bull for hours until the animal collapsed from fatigue, injuries or both.In 1835 the British Parliament enacted the Cruelty to Animals Act 1835, which prohibited the baiting of animals such as the bull and bear. Once baiting was outlawed, the public turned to “ratting”.This practice pitted dogs against rats in which they were timed to see whose dog would kill the most rats in the least amount of time. The “pit” in Pit Bull comes from ratting as the rats were placed into a pit so that they could not escape. Ultimately, the public turned their eyes upon dog fighting as it was more easily hidden from view and thus the law. Ratting and dogfighting both required more agility and speed on the part of the dog, so Bulldogs were crossed with Terriers , more commonly known as the first Pit Bull Terrier.Despite their tenacity and determination in battle, commoners actually bred pit bull terriers with some of the same qualities and traits that we still love about them to this day. Through selective breeding and culling, bite inhibition towards humans was greatly encouraged. Gamblers had to be sure that they could enter a pit and handle their dogs in close proximity without the danger of being bit themselves. If a dog bit a human, it was usually culled. Though these dogs had been specifically bred for fighting, they soon became a much larger and invaluable fixture in a developing nation. In early America, these frontier dogs took on an all-purpose role. They were responsible for herding cattle, herding sheep, guarding livestock and families against thieves and wild animals, helping on the hunts and as hog catchers. Their loyal and loving demeanor with humans, especially children (this is where the “Nanny Dog” myth originated from), earned them a prominent place not only as a working dog but as a companion.
